subtopic_detail: next investigation for a six week old with a raised conjugated bilirubin fraction after an ultrasound that failed to visualise the gallbladder
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional hospital reviewing a six week old breastfed girl referred because she is still yellow. She was born at term, is gaining weight along the tenth centile line, and feeds well.

Her mother says the nappies have been staining orange and that the last few dirty nappies have been the colour of putty rather than mustard. Total serum bilirubin is 148 micromol/L with a conjugated fraction of 68 micromol/L. Alanine aminotransferase is 128 units/L (5-45) and gamma glutamyl transferase is 410 units/L (5-45). Her international normalised ratio is 1.1, her newborn screening card was normal, and a urine culture is negative. An abdominal ultrasound performed this morning after four hours of fasting reports that the gallbladder was not visualised and that the liver is of normal echotexture with no cyst.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced sclerae, liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin and firm, spleen not palpable, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 68 micromol/L, alanine aminotransferase 128 units/L (5-45), gamma glutamyl transferase 410 units/L (5-45), international normalised ratio 1.1
data_table.Imaging: Abdominal ultrasound after four hours fasting: gallbladder not visualised, normal liver echotexture, no choledochal cyst

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate transfer to a paediatric liver unit for intraoperative cholangiography and liver biopsy
options.rationale: A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent with pale stools and a non-visualised gallbladder is obstructive cholestasis until disproven, and the definitive test is operative cholangiography with biopsy at a specialist centre. The urgency is driven by the fact that portoenterostomy performed before around sixty days of age gives far better bile drainage than surgery after that point. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice

options.text: Repeat the abdominal ultrasound after a six hour fast before making any referral decision
options.rationale: Fasting technique does affect gallbladder visualisation and a repeat scan is sometimes useful, but a normal ultrasound never excludes the diagnosis and repeating it costs days inside a narrow surgical window. Ultrasound is best used to find the alternative lesions such as a choledochal cyst. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice

options.text: Arrange a hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scan after five days of phenobarbitone pre-treatment
options.rationale: Radionuclide scanning has largely fallen out of favour because it is highly sensitive but poorly specific, and the phenobarbitone priming period adds close to a week of delay. It cannot exclude the diagnosis when it is abnormal, so the patient ends up at cholangiography regardless. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice

options.text: Reassure the family that this is breast milk jaundice and review the bilirubin again in two weeks
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and by definition has a conjugated fraction below 20 per cent with normal stool colour, so this infant fails both criteria. The near pair matters because a well feeding thriving baby looks reassuring and that is how the diagnosis is missed. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and fat soluble vitamin supplementation and review in the clinic weekly
options.rationale: Supportive nutritional and choleretic therapy belongs after the cause is established, and fat soluble vitamin replacement is certainly needed in prolonged cholestasis. Beginning it alone treats the consequences of obstruction while the window for surgery closes. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice)
source_refs: Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice

explanation.summary: Any infant still jaundiced at fourteen days of age needs a split bilirubin, and a conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total defines cholestasis that is never physiological. Pale acholic stools and dark urine point to obstruction, and a non-visualised gallbladder on a fasted ultrasound supports it although a normal scan would not exclude it. The definitive investigation is intraoperative cholangiography with liver biopsy at a paediatric liver centre, arranged without delay. Outcome after Kasai portoenterostomy falls sharply once the infant passes about sixty days, so referral is measured in days rather than weeks.
key_points: Jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days requires a split bilirubin, not observation
A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of total bilirubin is always pathological
Pale stools with dark urine indicate obstruction until proven otherwise
A normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary atresia; cholangiography is definitive
Portoenterostomy before about sixty days gives markedly better bile drainage
explanation.pearls: Ask the parents to compare the nappy against a printed stool colour chart rather than asking whether the stools look pale, because parental description alone misses about a third of acholic stools. A normal coagulation profile is reassuring only transiently: vitamin K dependent factors fall within weeks in cholestasis, so give intramuscular vitamin K before any biopsy is contemplated.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice
Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice

subtopic_detail: an adolescent with referred knee pain and an externally rotated leg whose frontal hip radiograph was reported as normal
stem:
You are the registrar in a suburban emergency department. A 13-year-old boy has had a dull ache in his left knee for six weeks, with no injury, no swelling and no locking. His general practitioner arranged a knee radiograph that was normal and started him on ibuprofen, which has not helped. He has been limping for the past fortnight and it is worse after football training.

He is afebrile and has been systemically well, with no rash, no other joint symptoms and no weight loss. His body mass index is on the 97th centile. Examination of the knee is entirely normal with a full painless range and no effusion. When you flex the left hip, the leg falls into obligatory external rotation, and internal rotation of the left hip is limited to 10 degrees compared with 40 degrees on the right. A frontal pelvic radiograph taken an hour ago has been reported as showing no fracture and normal joint spaces.

data_table.Examination: Normal knee examination with full painless range, left hip internal rotation 10 degrees versus 40 degrees on the right, obligatory external rotation on hip flexion
data_table.Investigations: Inflammatory markers not yet available, afebrile throughout
data_table.Imaging: Frontal pelvic radiograph: reported as no fracture, normal joint spaces

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange screening bloods for juvenile arthritis and review once the antinuclear antibody result returns
options.rationale: An inflammatory arthropathy would be expected to produce joint swelling, morning stiffness or involvement elsewhere, none of which are present. Serology has no role in a mechanical presentation and delays the imaging that will make the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute Limp

options.text: Request frog leg lateral views of both hips and make him strictly non-weight-bearing meanwhile
options.rationale: A frontal film misses early posterior slip of the femoral epiphysis in a substantial minority of cases, and the lateral projection is where the displacement is seen. Non-weight-bearing begins immediately on clinical suspicion because continued loading can convert a stable slip into an unstable one with a much higher rate of avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Request a magnetic resonance scan of the left hip and allow weight bearing as tolerated meanwhile
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance detects a pre-slip and is useful when plain films are genuinely normal, but it is not the immediate next test and permitting weight bearing while awaiting it is the part that causes harm. The lateral radiograph is faster and answers the question in most cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Request an ultrasound of the left hip to look for an effusion and review after inflammatory markers
options.rationale: Ultrasound answers the question of joint effusion, which serves transient synovitis and septic arthritis, and he is afebrile with six weeks of symptoms rather than days. The distinguishing relationship is that synovitis restricts rotation in all directions while a slip produces the characteristic obligatory external rotation on flexion. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute Limp

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for a patellofemoral rehabilitation program and review in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Anterior knee pain in an adolescent is frequently patellofemoral, but a normal knee examination with restricted hip rotation relocates the problem to the hip entirely. Six weeks of loaded rehabilitation is exactly the interval in which a stable slip progresses. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

explanation.summary: Knee pain in an adolescent with a normal knee examination should always redirect attention to the hip, because the obturator nerve refers hip pathology to the medial knee. Loss of internal rotation with obligatory external rotation as the hip is flexed is close to specific for slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and the risk factors of adolescence and raised body mass index fit. A frontal pelvic radiograph alone misses early slips because the displacement is posterior, so frog leg lateral views of both hips are required. Weight bearing must stop the moment the diagnosis is suspected, since progression from a stable to an unstable slip sharply increases the risk of avascular necrosis.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee pain
Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is the characteristic bedside sign
Frontal radiographs alone miss early posterior slips; frog leg laterals are essential
Image both hips, since bilateral involvement occurs in a substantial minority
Make the child non-weight-bearing on suspicion, before imaging confirms the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Trace Klein's line along the superior femoral neck on the frontal film: it should intersect part of the epiphysis, and failure to do so indicates a slip even when the report reads as normal. Screen for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency and renal osteodystrophy when a slip occurs outside the usual age band of ten to sixteen years or in a child of normal weight, since an endocrinopathy underlies a meaningful proportion of those cases.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
RCH CPG: Acute Limp

subtopic_detail: choice of imaging for suspected hip dysplasia first noticed at seven months when the femoral head has begun to ossify
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a seven month old girl for her routine check. Her mother has noticed that the creases on the back of the thighs do not match and that one leg seems shorter when she changes the nappy.

The pregnancy was complicated by breech presentation from 34 weeks, and she was born by elective caesarean at term. She has an older sister who wore a harness as a baby. On examination, with the hips and knees flexed and the feet together on the couch, the left knee sits visibly lower than the right. Abduction of the left hip is limited to 45 degrees compared with 75 degrees on the right. You feel no clunk on either side. Her tone, reflexes and spine are normal and she is meeting her developmental milestones.

data_table.Examination: Asymmetrical thigh creases, left knee lower than right on Galeazzi testing, left hip abduction 45 degrees versus 75 degrees on the right, no clunk elicited
data_table.Background: Breech from 34 weeks, first degree relative treated in a harness, normal neurological examination

options.text: No imaging, because the absence of a palpable clunk makes significant dysplasia unlikely here
options.rationale: The Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres lose their sensitivity after about three months because the hip becomes fixed rather than reducible, so a negative clunk in an older infant is expected and reassures nobody. Limited abduction and apparent limb shortening become the reliable signs at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: A limited computed tomography of the pelvis, because it defines acetabular version most precisely
options.rationale: Computed tomography gives a high radiation dose to the gonads of an infant girl for information that a plain film provides adequately before treatment. It has a role in postoperative assessment, not in diagnosis. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists: Paediatric Imaging Referral)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists: Paediatric Imaging Referral

options.text: A frontal pelvic radiograph, because the femoral head ossifies by around four to six months
options.rationale: Ultrasound depends on the femoral head being cartilaginous, and once the ossific nucleus appears at roughly four to six months it casts an acoustic shadow that obscures the acetabulum. From this age onward the plain radiograph is the investigation of choice, assessed using the acetabular index and Perkin's and Hilgenreiner's lines. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: A static and dynamic hip ultrasound, because it avoids ionising radiation in a young infant
options.rationale: Avoiding radiation is a sound instinct and ultrasound is genuinely the right test under about four months of age, but after ossification begins the image quality collapses and the study becomes unreliable. The distinguishing factor is the age of the child rather than a preference for one modality. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: A magnetic resonance scan of both hips, because it images cartilage and bone simultaneously
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance does image both tissues but requires sedation at this age and is reserved for assessing reduction after closed or open treatment. It is not a screening or first line diagnostic study. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: Breech presentation beyond 34 weeks and a first degree relative are the two strongest risk factors for hip dysplasia, and this girl has both. After about three months the reducible clunk disappears, so limited abduction and apparent femoral shortening on Galeazzi testing become the signs that matter. The imaging choice is governed purely by ossification of the femoral head, which occurs around four to six months: ultrasound before that point, plain radiography after it. At seven months the correct request is a frontal pelvic radiograph, with orthopaedic referral to follow because harness treatment is generally ineffective beyond six months.
key_points: Breech presentation after 34 weeks and a positive family history are the principal risk factors
Ortolani and Barlow testing loses sensitivity after about three months of age
Limited abduction and a positive Galeazzi sign replace the clunk in older infants
Ultrasound is the test under four months; plain radiography is the test after ossification
Pavlik harness treatment is generally ineffective beyond six months of age
explanation.pearls: Unilateral limitation of abduction to less than 60 degrees in an infant beyond three months should prompt imaging even when every other finding is normal, since it is the single most reliable late sign. Expect an acetabular index above 25 degrees at one year to indicate dysplasia, and remember that a hip which was normal on newborn ultrasound can still present late, so reassess abduction at every routine check until walking.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists: Paediatric Imaging Referral

subtopic_detail: ophthalmology surveillance interval for a young girl with persistent knee swelling and a positive antinuclear antibody who has no eye symptoms
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic. A 3-year-old girl has had a swollen right knee for four months. Her parents noticed she was stiff and reluctant to walk for the first hour each morning, and then ran about normally by lunchtime. She has had no fever, no rash, no weight loss and no night pain that wakes her.

On examination the right knee has a moderate effusion with a fixed flexion deformity of 10 degrees, and there is a smaller effusion at the right ankle. No other joint is involved. Her growth is tracking along the 50th centile. Full blood count, C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate are within normal limits, blood cultures are negative, and antinuclear antibody is positive at a titre of 1 in 320. Rheumatoid factor is negative. Her eyes are white and painless and her parents have noticed no visual difficulty.

data_table.Examination: Right knee effusion with 10 degree fixed flexion, small right ankle effusion, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, white painless eyes
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate within normal limits, antinuclear antibody positive at 1 in 320, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What eye care would you arrange?

options.text: Visual acuity testing at each clinic visit, with ophthalmology referral only if the acuity falls
options.rationale: Acuity remains normal until the inflammation has already caused structural damage, so waiting for it to fall means referring after the harm is done. Acuity testing is a useful adjunct but cannot substitute for the slit lamp. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis

options.text: Slit lamp examination now, with further screening arranged only if the arthritis remains active
options.rationale: Eye inflammation runs a course independent of joint activity and commonly flares while the joints are quiet, so tying surveillance to arthritis activity is unsafe. Screening continues for years after the arthritis settles. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

options.text: Dilated fundoscopy by the treating paediatrician at each visit, with referral if a red reflex is lost
options.rationale: Fundoscopy examines the posterior segment, whereas this uveitis is anterior and its cells and flare are visible only through a slit lamp. Loss of the red reflex indicates established cataract, which is a late complication rather than a screening finding. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis

options.text: Slit lamp examination now and then three monthly, because her profile carries the highest uveitis risk
options.rationale: Chronic anterior uveitis in this form of childhood arthritis is asymptomatic, produces no redness or pain, and is detected only on slit lamp examination, so screening intervals are set by risk rather than by symptoms. A girl under seven with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody sits in the highest risk band and is screened three monthly. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

options.text: Slit lamp examination now and then twelve monthly, because her eyes are currently white and painless
options.rationale: Twelve monthly screening applies to the lowest risk groups such as older children with systemic onset disease, and using the absence of symptoms to set the interval defeats the purpose of screening. The whole reason this uveitis is dangerous is that it is silent until synechiae or cataract have formed. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

explanation.summary: Persistent arthritis of four or fewer joints for more than six weeks in a child under sixteen, with normal inflammatory markers and no systemic features, describes oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The complication that determines long term disability is chronic anterior uveitis, which is entirely asymptomatic with a white quiet eye and is detected only by slit lamp examination. Risk is stratified by age at onset, disease subtype and antinuclear antibody status, and a young girl with oligoarticular disease and a positive antibody falls into the highest risk band requiring three monthly screening. Eye disease flares independently of joint activity, so screening continues regardless of how the arthritis behaves.
key_points: Oligoarticular disease with a positive antinuclear antibody in a young child is the highest uveitis risk group
The uveitis is asymptomatic with a white eye and normal acuity until damage is established
Slit lamp examination is the only adequate screening test
Eye and joint activity are independent, so surveillance is not tied to arthritis control
Normal inflammatory markers do not argue against the diagnosis in oligoarticular disease
explanation.pearls: Screen three monthly for a girl under seven with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody, six monthly when the antibody is negative or onset is later, and twelve monthly for systemic onset disease, continuing for at least four years after arthritis remission. Intra-articular corticosteroid injection is the usual first treatment for a single persistently swollen joint and often achieves prolonged remission without any systemic agent.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis

subtopic_detail: timing of a delayed live viral vaccine in a child who has just finished a prolonged high dose oral corticosteroid course
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar running a general clinic. A 2-year-old boy has just completed an eight week course of oral prednisolone at 2 mg/kg daily for steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome, finishing his last tapering dose four days ago. He is now in remission with no proteinuria on home dipstick testing for three weeks.

His parents want to catch up the measles, mumps and rubella and varicella vaccines that were deferred when he became unwell before his eighteen month visit. He has had all his inactivated vaccines on schedule. He is otherwise well, growing normally, taking no other immunosuppressive medication, and his full blood count and albumin are within normal limits. His four year old sister attends childcare, where a case of measles was notified in another room three weeks ago, and the family is planning to travel to Bali in five months.

data_table.Examination: Well, no oedema, no cushingoid features, growth along the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and albumin within normal limits, urine dipstick negative for protein for three weeks
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for eight weeks, completed four days ago, no other immunosuppressant

lead_in: When should the live vaccines be given?

options.text: Immediately at this visit, since the course has finished and he is currently in clinical remission
options.rationale: Clinical remission is not the same as restored cell mediated immunity, and vaccinating within days of stopping high dose steroid risks disseminated infection from the attenuated virus. The deferral is tied to the steroid, not to disease activity. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook

options.text: After a three month interval from the last corticosteroid dose, giving both live vaccines together
options.rationale: Three months is the interval used after more profound immunosuppression such as chemotherapy or biologic therapy, and applying it here delays protection unnecessarily. The distinguishing factor is the depth and type of immunosuppression rather than its duration alone. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook

options.text: After a one month interval, giving the vaccines four weeks apart rather than on the same day
options.rationale: The timing is right but separating the two live vaccines unnecessarily is wrong, because they may be co-administered at different sites. The four week rule applies only when two live parenteral vaccines are not given on the same day. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook

options.text: Never, because a history of steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome is a permanent contraindication
options.rationale: Nephrotic syndrome is not a contraindication to any vaccine, and these children in fact need particular attention to pneumococcal and varicella protection because of their infection risk. The only contraindication relates to the timing of immunosuppressive therapy. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome

options.text: After a one month interval from the last corticosteroid dose, giving both live vaccines together
options.rationale: A course of 2 mg/kg daily of prednisolone for more than fourteen days counts as high dose immunosuppression, and Australian practice is to defer live vaccines for one month after it stops so that immune competence is restored. Measles, mumps and rubella and varicella vaccines may be given on the same day at different sites, which is the efficient choice ahead of his travel. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook

explanation.summary: Prednisolone at 2 mg/kg daily, or more than 20 mg daily in a child over 10 kg, given for fourteen days or longer is considered high dose immunosuppression for vaccination purposes. Live attenuated vaccines are deferred until one month after such a course finishes, whereas the three month deferral belongs to chemotherapy and biologic agents. Measles, mumps and rubella and varicella vaccines may be given on the same day at separate sites, and if they are not, they must be separated by at least four weeks. Nephrotic syndrome itself is never a contraindication, and these children benefit particularly from complete varicella and pneumococcal protection.
key_points: Prednisolone at or above 2 mg/kg daily for fourteen days or more counts as high dose immunosuppression
Defer live vaccines for one month after stopping high dose corticosteroid
Three month deferral applies after chemotherapy or biologic therapy, not after steroids alone
Two live parenteral vaccines are given the same day or separated by at least four weeks
Nephrotic syndrome is an indication for careful catch up, not a contraindication
explanation.pearls: Inactivated vaccines can be given at any point during or after immunosuppression, so never delay the influenza or pneumococcal dose while waiting out a steroid course, even though the response may be blunted. For a documented measles exposure in a susceptible immunosuppressed child, normal human immunoglobulin within six days is the protection strategy rather than vaccine, because the live vaccine is contraindicated during the deferral window.

sources.label: Australian Immunisation Handbook
Kidney Health Australia: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome

subtopic_detail: an adolescent with sudden scrotal pain whose ultrasound is reported as showing preserved arterial flow
stem:
You are the registrar in the emergency department at nine in the evening. A 13-year-old boy woke at seven o'clock this morning with sudden severe pain in the left side of the scrotum and vomited twice. He did not tell anyone until after school because he was embarrassed, and the pain is now somewhat less than it was.

He is afebrile with no urinary symptoms and no discharge. The left hemiscrotum is swollen and red, the left testis sits higher than the right and lies transversely, and there is no cremasteric reflex on the left. Elevating the testis does not relieve the pain. Urinalysis shows no leucocytes and no nitrites. A scrotal ultrasound performed twenty minutes ago is reported as showing a swollen left testis with an oedematous epididymis, some peripheral arterial flow present and a small reactive hydrocele. The surgical registrar is in theatre and asks for your recommendation.

data_table.Examination: Left hemiscrotum swollen and erythematous, left testis high riding and transverse, absent left cremasteric reflex, no relief on elevation
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for leucocytes and nitrites
data_table.Imaging: Scrotal ultrasound: swollen left testis, oedematous epididymis, peripheral arterial flow present, small reactive hydrocele

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange immediate surgical exploration of the scrotum with bilateral fixation if torsion is found
options.rationale: A high riding transverse testis with an absent cremasteric reflex after abrupt onset pain and vomiting is a clinical diagnosis of torsion, and preserved flow on ultrasound does not exclude it because partial or intermittent torsion and residual capsular flow are both well described. Exploration with fixation of both sides is the only action that can salvage the testis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain

options.text: Treat with oral antibiotics for epididymo-orchitis and arrange urology review within forty eight hours
options.rationale: Epididymo-orchitis is the near pair and would be supported by gradual onset, fever, pyuria and relief on elevation, none of which are present here. Treating him as an infection on the basis of an oedematous epididymis on ultrasound is how torsion is missed. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain

options.text: Observe overnight with analgesia and repeat the scrotal ultrasound in the morning before deciding
options.rationale: Salvage rates fall steeply beyond six hours and he is already fourteen hours in, so an overnight delay for a repeat scan effectively decides against the testis. Reducing pain over time reflects ischaemic nerve death rather than improvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain

options.text: Attempt manual detorsion in the emergency department and discharge him if the pain fully settles
options.rationale: Manual detorsion is a reasonable temporising manoeuvre while theatre is prepared, but it is never definitive because the underlying bell clapper anomaly remains and retorsion is common. Discharge without fixation leaves him at immediate risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain

options.text: Request a radionuclide scrotal perfusion scan to resolve the discrepancy between examination and ultrasound
options.rationale: Nuclear imaging adds hours and its result would not override a bedside examination this characteristic. Imaging is for the equivocal presentation, and this one is not equivocal. (Source: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute Scrotum)
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute Scrotum

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis and an operative emergency, and imaging exists to support it rather than to overrule it. Abrupt severe pain with vomiting, a high riding transverse testis, an absent cremasteric reflex and no relief on elevation are together highly predictive. Preserved arterial flow on ultrasound occurs with partial torsion, intermittent torsion and early presentations, so a reassuring scan in a patient with these findings must not delay theatre. Delayed presentation from embarrassment is common in this age group and reduced pain often signals ischaemic nerve death rather than resolution, so exploration is still warranted.
key_points: Torsion is diagnosed clinically; ultrasound cannot exclude it when examination is characteristic
Absent cremasteric reflex with a high riding transverse testis is the key sign cluster
Relief on elevation favours epididymo-orchitis, the principal near pair
Salvage falls sharply beyond six hours, so exploration is not deferred for further imaging
Both testes are fixed at operation because the underlying anomaly is bilateral
explanation.pearls: Torsion of the appendix testis is the commonest mimic in this age group and shows a focal tender blue dot at the upper pole with a normal cremasteric reflex, and it is managed with analgesia alone. Even beyond twenty four hours, explore rather than assume the testis is lost: the contralateral side still requires fixation, and documented necrosis at operation is far better than an unexplored scrotum for the boy's future fertility discussion.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain
Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute Scrotum

subtopic_detail: purulent eye discharge appearing on the third day of life in a baby whose mother declined antenatal screening
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the postnatal ward. A baby boy born at term by normal vaginal delivery is now sixty hours old. Since this morning both eyelids have become markedly swollen and there is thick yellow discharge that reaccumulates within minutes of being wiped away.

His mother booked late in the pregnancy, declined the offered antenatal infection screening, and reported an untreated vaginal discharge in the third trimester. The baby is feeding well, afebrile, and the rest of the examination is normal. The lids are tense and difficult to part, the conjunctivae are intensely injected and chemotic, and the cornea appears clear on the limited view you can obtain. A Gram stain of the discharge sent urgently shows numerous polymorphonuclear cells with intracellular Gram negative diplococci. Nucleic acid testing of the same swab is pending.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral tense lid oedema, marked conjunctival injection and chemosis, copious purulent discharge, cornea clear on limited view
data_table.Investigations: Gram stain of discharge: numerous polymorphonuclear cells with intracellular Gram negative diplococci, nucleic acid testing pending
data_table.Background: Term normal vaginal delivery, antenatal screening declined, untreated third trimester vaginal discharge

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Await the nucleic acid testing result before starting any antimicrobial and continue saline irrigation
options.rationale: The Gram stain has already given an actionable answer and waiting a further day for confirmation risks the cornea. Nucleic acid testing remains valuable for confirming the organism and for contact tracing, but it does not gate treatment. (Source: Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Neonatal Conjunctivitis)
source_refs: Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Neonatal Conjunctivitis

options.text: Admit for intravenous third generation cephalosporin with hourly saline eye irrigation and ophthalmology review
options.rationale: Intracellular Gram negative diplococci on day three with hyperacute purulent discharge and lid oedema is gonococcal ophthalmia, which perforates the cornea within twenty four to forty eight hours if treated topically alone. Systemic cephalosporin plus frequent saline irrigation to clear the enzyme rich discharge, with urgent ophthalmology involvement, is the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Start oral erythromycin for fourteen days with saline eye irrigation and review in the clinic in two days
options.rationale: Fourteen days of oral erythromycin is the correct regimen for chlamydial ophthalmia, which is the other vertically acquired cause but presents at five to fourteen days with a more mucopurulent and less explosive discharge. The distinguishing relationship is the organism on Gram stain and the timing of onset. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Start topical chloramphenicol drops with saline eye irrigation and review in the clinic in two days
options.rationale: Topical therapy alone does not reach the systemic sites this organism seeds, including joints and the bloodstream, and does not prevent corneal perforation. Chloramphenicol is appropriate for ordinary bacterial conjunctivitis in an older infant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Reassure the family this is chemical irritation from birth prophylaxis and continue saline irrigation only
options.rationale: Chemical conjunctivitis appears within the first twenty four hours and settles spontaneously, and it produces a watery rather than thick purulent discharge. Gram negative diplococci on the stain exclude it outright. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: Neonatal conjunctivitis is stratified by the day of onset and the organism, because management differs sharply. Chemical irritation appears in the first twenty four hours, gonococcal disease at two to five days with hyperacute purulent discharge and tense lid oedema, and chlamydial disease at five to fourteen days with a more indolent course. Intracellular Gram negative diplococci confirm the gonococcal diagnosis, which threatens the cornea within a day or two and requires systemic third generation cephalosporin rather than topical therapy. Frequent saline irrigation removes the proteolytic enzyme laden discharge, and both parents require testing and treatment.
key_points: Day of onset narrows the cause: chemical under one day, gonococcal two to five, chlamydial five to fourteen
Intracellular Gram negative diplococci mandate systemic, not topical, therapy
Corneal perforation can occur within twenty four to forty eight hours in gonococcal disease
Hourly saline irrigation is part of treatment, not merely comfort care
Chlamydial ophthalmia requires oral erythromycin because topical treatment leaves nasopharyngeal carriage
explanation.pearls: Always treat the parents as well as the baby and notify as required, since the infection is sexually transmitted and reinfection of the newborn from an untreated carer is common. A baby treated topically for chlamydial conjunctivitis still develops pneumonitis at four to twelve weeks, which is why the oral course is mandatory even when the eye looks better.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Neonatal Conjunctivitis

subtopic_detail: secondary prophylaxis decision after a first episode of migratory polyarthritis with a raised streptococcal titre in a high incidence remote community
stem:
You are the medical officer at a remote clinic in the Northern Territory. A 9-year-old Aboriginal boy is brought in with three weeks of joint pain that began in the left ankle, settled, then moved to the right knee and now affects the left wrist. Each joint was hot and swollen for two or three days before improving.

He had a sore throat about five weeks ago that was not treated. He has had intermittent fevers and is tired and off his food. His temperature is 38.1 degrees Celsius with other vital signs within normal limits. There is a soft apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla that was not documented at his school health check last year. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 78 mm/h (<15), C-reactive protein 62 mg/L (<5), and antistreptolysin O titre is 620 IU/mL with an elevated anti-DNase B. The electrocardiogram shows a PR interval of 0.20 seconds, and an echocardiogram shows mild mitral regurgitation with no other abnormality.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius, other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Migratory large joint arthritis now in the left wrist, new soft apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla, no rash, no nodules
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 78 mm/h (<15), C-reactive protein 62 mg/L (<5), antistreptolysin O 620 IU/mL with elevated anti-DNase B
data_table.Cardiac: Electrocardiogram PR interval 0.20 seconds; echocardiogram shows mild mitral regurgitation

lead_in: What is the most important element of his ongoing management?

options.text: Oral corticosteroid for the carditis with echocardiographic review at the end of the treatment course
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is considered only in severe carditis with heart failure, and mild mitral regurgitation with a normal ventricle does not reach that bar. It also addresses this episode rather than the recurrences that determine long term valve damage. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.text: Annual echocardiographic surveillance alone, with antibiotics reserved for any future sore throat
options.rationale: Surveillance detects deterioration but does nothing to prevent it, and treating sore throats as they arise fails because many streptococcal infections are subclinical. The near pair is primary prevention in a child with no prior episode, where treating symptomatic pharyngitis is indeed the strategy. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.text: Four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin continued for at least ten years or to age 21
options.rationale: Once acute rheumatic fever is diagnosed, long term secondary prophylaxis is the single intervention that changes the trajectory, because each recurrence worsens valve damage. Australian guidance sets the minimum duration at ten years from the last episode or until age 21, whichever is longer, with longer courses when carditis is present. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.text: A ten day course of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin to eradicate the organism with no further prophylaxis
options.rationale: Eradication of residual pharyngeal carriage is part of initial management but treats only this episode, and stopping there leaves him fully exposed to the recurrences that cause chronic valve disease. Primary treatment and secondary prophylaxis are separate interventions with different durations. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.text: High dose aspirin until the inflammatory markers normalise, with clinical review at that point
options.rationale: Anti-inflammatory therapy relieves the arthritis and is appropriate symptomatic treatment, but it has no effect on valve outcome or recurrence risk. Reviewing only when markers normalise misses the point that prophylaxis must continue for years. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

explanation.summary: Migratory polyarthritis, fever, a new mitral regurgitant murmur, a prolonged PR interval and raised streptococcal serology in a child from a high incidence community meet the Australian criteria for acute rheumatic fever. Initial management includes penicillin to clear residual carriage and anti-inflammatory therapy for the arthritis, but neither changes long term outcome. Secondary prophylaxis with four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin is the intervention that prevents recurrences, and recurrences are what convert mild regurgitation into established rheumatic heart disease. Minimum duration is ten years from the last episode or until age 21, whichever is longer, and it is extended where carditis has occurred.
key_points: Australian criteria apply a high risk definition in populations with high incidence
A prolonged PR interval counts as a minor criterion and supports carditis
Secondary prophylaxis, not the treatment of this episode, determines valve outcome
Four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin is the standard regimen
Minimum duration is ten years or until age 21, whichever is longer, and longer with carditis
explanation.pearls: Register every case with the state or territory rheumatic heart disease control program on the day of diagnosis, because recall for four weekly injections depends on that register far more than on any single clinic's follow up. Salicylates should be withheld until the arthritis pattern has been documented, since rapid symptomatic response can obscure the migratory course that the diagnosis depends upon.

sources.label: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

subtopic_detail: displaced elbow fracture in a child with an absent radial pulse but a hand that remains warm and well perfused
stem:
You are the registrar in a metropolitan emergency department. A 6-year-old girl fell from the monkey bars onto an outstretched hand ninety minutes ago and has an obviously deformed right elbow. Radiographs show a completely displaced supracondylar humeral fracture with posterolateral displacement of the distal fragment.

On examination there is marked swelling at the elbow with puckering of the skin over the anterior crease. The radial pulse is not palpable and cannot be detected on handheld Doppler. Her hand is warm and pink with a capillary refill of two seconds, and the pulse oximeter on the index finger reads 99 per cent with a good trace. She can flex and extend her fingers and thumb and reports normal sensation in all three nerve distributions. She has increasing pain and has needed two doses of analgesia. The orthopaedic registrar is forty minutes away and asks what you recommend.

data_table.Examination: Gross elbow swelling with anterior skin puckering, radial pulse impalpable and absent on Doppler, hand warm and pink with capillary refill two seconds
data_table.Neurological: Intact flexion and extension of fingers and thumb, normal sensation in median, ulnar and radial distributions
data_table.Imaging: Radiographs: completely displaced supracondylar humeral fracture with posterolateral displacement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a backslab in ninety degrees of flexion and admit for hourly neurovascular observation overnight
options.rationale: Flexion beyond about forty degrees compresses the antecubital fossa and can convert a perfused pulseless limb into an ischaemic one, and delaying reduction overnight risks compartment syndrome. Immobilisation in modest flexion is a transport measure, not a definitive plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus

options.text: Arrange computed tomography angiography of the arm to define the arterial injury before theatre
options.rationale: Angiography rarely changes the plan because the fracture must be reduced whatever it shows, and the delay it introduces is the harm. Imaging the vessel belongs after reduction in the child whose perfusion has not returned. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus

options.text: Perform closed reduction under procedural sedation in the emergency department and discharge if perfused
options.rationale: A completely displaced fracture is inherently unstable and requires percutaneous wire fixation to hold the reduction, so a closed manipulation without fixation will redisplace. Discharging a child with this injury also forfeits the observation period that compartment syndrome demands. (Source: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric Trauma)
source_refs: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric Trauma

options.text: Urgent operative reduction and fixation, with vascular assessment repeated once the fracture is reduced
options.rationale: A completely displaced supracondylar fracture with an absent pulse is a surgical emergency regardless of how well the hand looks, because the brachial artery is tethered or kinked by the displaced fragment and reduction usually restores flow. Perfusion is reassessed after reduction, and vascular exploration is reserved for the hand that remains pulseless and poorly perfused at that point. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus

options.text: Immediate vascular surgical exploration of the brachial artery before any attempt at fracture reduction
options.rationale: Exploring the artery before reduction addresses a vessel whose problem is usually mechanical tethering that reduction relieves, and it exposes the child to an operation that most do not need. Exploration is the correct step only for the hand that is pale and pulseless after reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus

explanation.summary: Supracondylar fractures are stratified by displacement, and a completely displaced fracture with an absent pulse goes to theatre urgently whatever the hand looks like. The critical distinction is between the pink pulseless hand, where the artery is usually kinked or in spasm around the displaced fragment and reduction restores flow, and the white pulseless hand, which is true ischaemia requiring vascular involvement from the outset. Angiography and pre-reduction exploration both introduce delay without changing the fact that the fracture must be reduced. Anterior skin puckering signals brachialis entrapment and predicts that closed reduction may fail, which is another reason the child belongs in theatre rather than in the emergency department.
key_points: A completely displaced supracondylar fracture with an absent pulse is an operative emergency
Reduction commonly restores flow because the artery is tethered rather than transected
Reassess perfusion after reduction; explore only the hand that stays white and pulseless
Avoid flexing the elbow beyond about forty degrees when splinting, since it compresses the fossa
Anterior skin puckering suggests brachialis entrapment and predicts failure of closed reduction
explanation.pearls: The anterior interosseous nerve is the most commonly injured and is missed on a standard sensory examination because it is purely motor: ask the child to make an oval by pinching the tip of the thumb against the tip of the index finger. Escalating pain requiring repeated analgesia in the hours after injury is the earliest sign of compartment syndrome in a child, and it precedes pulselessness by hours.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric Trauma

subtopic_detail: persistent unilateral wheeze weeks after a choking episode in a toddler whose chest radiograph on inspiration is reported as normal
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic. A 2-year-old boy has been treated for presumed asthma for five weeks with inhaled salbutamol and a two week course of oral prednisolone, with no improvement. His parents cannot recall a definite choking episode but mention that his symptoms began the afternoon he was eating a bowl of mixed nuts at a family lunch and coughed hard for a few minutes.

He has no fever and has never had eczema, allergic rhinitis or wheeze before this illness, and there is no family history of atopy. His growth is normal. On auscultation there is a monophonic wheeze localised to the right chest with reduced air entry at the right base, and the left chest is clear. His observations are within normal limits with SpO2 97 per cent on room air. An inspiratory chest radiograph is reported as showing no focal consolidation, no collapse and symmetrical lung fields.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits, SpO2 97 per cent on room air
data_table.Examination: Monophonic wheeze localised to the right chest, reduced right basal air entry, left chest clear, no clubbing
data_table.Background: No personal or family history of atopy, no fever, normal growth, no response to bronchodilator or oral corticosteroid
data_table.Imaging: Inspiratory chest radiograph: no consolidation, no collapse, symmetrical lung fields

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request expiratory or lateral decubitus chest radiographs and reassess once those films are available
options.rationale: Additional projections genuinely increase sensitivity by demonstrating air trapping, and are worth obtaining, but a negative result would not change the plan because the clinical picture already mandates airway inspection. Relying on them risks a falsely reassuring report in a poorly cooperative toddler. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled Foreign Body)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inhaled Foreign Body

options.text: Escalate to inhaled corticosteroid with a spacer and review the response in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: Preventer therapy assumes an asthma diagnosis that this child does not fit, given no atopy, no prior wheeze, a fixed unilateral monophonic wheeze and no response to a steroid course already given. Another four weeks of retained organic material produces granulation tissue and bronchiectasis. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Asthma

options.text: Perform flexible bronchoscopy in the clinic under sedation to inspect the airway and remove any object
options.rationale: Flexible bronchoscopy is useful for inspection and lavage but has no adequate instrument channel for retrieving a solid object and offers no airway control if the object dislodges. The distinguishing relationship is that the rigid scope simultaneously ventilates and permits forceps retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled Foreign Body)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inhaled Foreign Body

options.text: Request chest physiotherapy with postural drainage and a course of oral antibiotics for the right base
options.rationale: Physiotherapy risks dislodging an object into the trachea where it can obstruct completely, and antibiotics treat a secondary infection without removing the cause. Neither addresses the mechanical obstruction. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Paediatric Airway)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Paediatric Airway

options.text: Refer for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia for airway inspection and possible retrieval
options.rationale: A localised monophonic wheeze that does not respond to bronchodilator or corticosteroid in a toddler with a plausible aspiration event is an inhaled foreign body until the airway is inspected, and a normal inspiratory film does not exclude it because a ball valve obstruction shows only on expiration. Rigid bronchoscopy is both the diagnostic and the therapeutic procedure. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled Foreign Body)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inhaled Foreign Body

explanation.summary: Fixed, localised, monophonic wheeze in a toddler that does not respond to bronchodilator or corticosteroid is an airway obstruction until proven otherwise, and asthma is very unlikely without atopy or prior episodes. A witnessed choking event is absent in a large minority of cases, so a plausible circumstantial history such as eating nuts carries real weight. An inspiratory chest radiograph is normal in up to a third of inhaled foreign bodies because most organic objects are radiolucent and the ball valve effect only shows as air trapping on expiration. Rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic and provides airway control, which flexible bronchoscopy does not.
key_points: A fixed monophonic unilateral wheeze is mechanical obstruction, not bronchospasm
Absence of a witnessed choking episode does not exclude an inhaled foreign body
A normal inspiratory chest radiograph is common because most objects are radiolucent
Rigid bronchoscopy allows simultaneous ventilation and instrumented retrieval
Chest physiotherapy risks converting partial to complete obstruction
explanation.pearls: Expiratory or lateral decubitus films raise sensitivity by demonstrating air trapping on the affected side, where the dependent lung fails to deflate, but a negative study never overturns a clinical suspicion strong enough to warrant bronchoscopy. Peanut is the commonest culprit in Australian children and is particularly damaging because the oil provokes an intense chemical bronchitis within days, so delay converts a simple retrieval into a granulation filled airway.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Inhaled Foreign Body
RCH CPG: Asthma
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Paediatric Airway

subtopic_detail: encephalopathy on the fourth day of life with a respiratory alkalosis and a very high ammonia after an uncomplicated term birth
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a level four regional nursery. A term boy, born after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery with Apgar scores of nine and nine, fed well for the first two days and was discharged. He returned this morning, on day four, because he had become increasingly sleepy overnight, vomited three times and would not attach to the breast.

He is now poorly responsive with intermittent lip smacking and cycling movements of his legs, and his tone is markedly reduced. His temperature is 36.4 degrees Celsius with other observations within normal limits, and his respiratory rate is 72 per minute with no recession and clear lungs. Blood glucose is 3.6 mmol/L. A capillary blood gas shows pH 7.51, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 26 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L and lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). Urine ketones are negative. Plasma ammonia, collected free flowing on ice and run immediately, is 620 micromol/L (<100). Sodium, potassium, calcium and the full blood count are within normal limits, and there is no family history of note.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius, respiratory rate 72 per minute, other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Poorly responsive, markedly reduced tone, intermittent lip smacking and leg cycling, chest clear with no recession, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Plasma ammonia 620 micromol/L (<100), glucose 3.6 mmol/L, urine ketones negative, sodium, potassium, calcium and full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Blood gas: pH 7.51, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 26 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Stop all protein intake, start high rate intravenous dextrose with lipid, and arrange dialysis transfer
options.rationale: A normal anion gap with a respiratory alkalosis, absent ketones, normal lactate and an ammonia above 500 micromol/L on day four points to a urea cycle defect rather than an organic acidaemia, and ammonia at this level is directly neurotoxic. Immediate management removes the nitrogen load, reverses catabolism with a high glucose infusion rate plus lipid, and transfers for haemodialysis, which clears ammonia far faster than scavengers alone. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism)
source_refs: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

options.text: Start full sepsis treatment with intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin and continue breastfeeding
options.rationale: Late onset sepsis is the correct parallel consideration and antibiotics should indeed be given while cultures are pending, but continuing enteral protein in the face of an ammonia of 620 micromol/L drives the encephalopathy further. Sepsis also does not produce this degree of hyperammonaemia with a normal lactate and normal white cell count. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Sepsis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal Sepsis

options.text: Load with intravenous phenobarbitone for the seizure activity and observe with two hourly ammonia levels
options.rationale: The subtle seizures are a manifestation of ammonia neurotoxicity and will not settle while the level stays above 500 micromol/L, so anticonvulsant alone treats the symptom. Serial monitoring without intervention wastes the hours in which neurological outcome is determined. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism)
source_refs: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

options.text: Give a 10 per cent dextrose bolus for hypoglycaemia and recheck the glucose and ammonia in one hour
options.rationale: A glucose of 3.6 mmol/L is acceptable on day four and is not the explanation for the encephalopathy, so treating it as the primary problem misreads the picture. Dextrose is central to management, but as a continuous high rate anticatabolic infusion rather than a single bolus. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Start intravenous sodium bicarbonate and fluid restriction while awaiting the newborn screening result
options.rationale: There is no acidosis to correct, since the gas shows an alkalotic pH driven by ammonia stimulated hyperventilation, and alkali would worsen it. Newborn screening results take days and several urea cycle defects are not reliably detected on it at all. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism)
source_refs: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

explanation.summary: A term baby who feeds normally for two days and then deteriorates with vomiting, encephalopathy and tachypnoea is following the classic latent interval of a metabolic disorder, because the protein load only accumulates after feeding is established. The blood gas is the discriminator: ammonia stimulates the respiratory centre and produces a respiratory alkalosis, whereas an organic acidaemia produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketosis, and both are absent here. An ammonia above 500 micromol/L is a neurological emergency in which the duration of exposure predicts outcome, so management runs in parallel rather than in sequence. Nitrogen intake stops, a high glucose infusion rate with lipid reverses catabolism, nitrogen scavengers are started on metabolic advice, and transfer for haemodialysis is arranged without waiting for a diagnosis.
key_points: A symptom free interval of one to three days followed by encephalopathy suggests a metabolic disorder
Respiratory alkalosis with normal lactate and absent ketones points away from organic acidaemia
Ammonia must be collected free flowing, on ice and run immediately or it reads falsely high
Ammonia above 500 micromol/L warrants dialysis planning, not scavengers alone
Treat empirically for sepsis in parallel, but stop all protein intake
explanation.pearls: Run dextrose at an infusion rate of about 8 to 10 mg/kg/min with intravenous lipid to shut down endogenous protein breakdown, because the baby's own muscle is the dominant nitrogen source once feeds have stopped. Neurological outcome correlates with the number of hours the ammonia spends above 300 micromol/L, so activate the retrieval service and the metabolic unit at the first result rather than after a confirmatory repeat.

sources.label: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism
RCH CPG: Neonatal Sepsis
RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia
